sentences: This is Death and the Maiden by Egon Schiele.
At the centre of a canvas 180 centimetres wide, two people embrace on a crumpled white sheet.
Around them lies rough, dark brown ground, with no sky and no horizon.
Look first at the man's eyes.
Wrapped in what looks like a dark monk's robe, he holds the woman, yet his wide eyes stare into empty space.
The man is a self-portrait of Schiele.
With one hand he cradles her red hair.
Yet the gesture feels less tender than heavy, almost like a final farewell.
Notice his long, bony fingers, spread wide across her head.
The woman clings to him with both arms, her face pressed against his chest.
She is Wally Neuzil, his partner and model for several years, the woman who had shared his life and work.
Her hands grip him as if she will not let go.
They met in 1911, and Wally stood by him even when he was briefly jailed.
But in 1915 Schiele became engaged to Edith Harms, a woman from a respectable middle-class family, and Wally left him at once.
He married Edith that June and was drafted into the First World War just three days later.
In his work of this period, death and love often appear together, and this painting followed straight after the break-up.
Her dress is made of short, sharp strokes of red, green and white.
Pressed against his dark, heavy robe, it looks like the warmth of a body that is still very much alive.
The background on the right is lumpy ground in browns and ochres.
It looks like rock and like crumpled cloth at the same time, as if the pair had nowhere solid in the world to lean.
The two bodies tilt across the white sheet as if about to slip.
Their unstable pose shows a fragile balance that seems ready to break at any moment.
Her legs are already sliding away to the lower right.
Schiele first called the picture Man and Girl, and also Entwined People.
The later title, Death and the Maiden, borrows a theme that goes back to the Renaissance, where death comes to claim a young woman.
After they parted, Wally trained as a nurse.
She died of scarlet fever in December 1917, aged twenty-three, while serving in the war.
The painting that holds their story is now in the Belvedere in Vienna.
Step back and look at the space between them.
Holding on, yet already letting go: in this moment, who is clinging to whom?
And which of them will be the first to let go?
